title: Phone call: older woman unwell with diarrhoea

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, is that Mrs Brackenbury?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, dear, speaking.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It's Dr Osei from the surgery, returning your son's call. Is it all right to talk?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes. Martin's here too, he's on the speakerphone.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Hello, doctor.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, Martin. Mrs Brackenbury, can you confirm your date of birth?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Third of March, 1941.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you. What's been happening?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've had the runs and I've been sick. I feel washed out.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long has this been going on?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Two days now. Since Monday.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How many times have you been sick today?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Twice this morning. Nothing since lunch.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And the diarrhoea, how many times?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Four or five times today.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any blood in it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Are you managing to drink?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Sips of water. I don't fancy much.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She's barely touched her tea all day.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: When did you last pass urine, and what colour was it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This morning. It was dark.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you feel dizzy when you stand up?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I hold onto the furniture.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you had any falls?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She had a fall last month, didn't you, Mum?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, Martin, that was Mrs Jenkins next door. I haven't fallen.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Oh, sorry, yes. That was Mrs Jenkins.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, no falls. Any tummy pain?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just crampy before I go.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Are you feeling confused at all? Martin, does she seem her usual self?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She's tired but she's making sense.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Let me go through your tablets. You take metformin?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, 500 twice a day.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Ramipril 5 milligrams?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And your water tablet, furosemide. How much do you take?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Two in the morning. No, one. The 40 milligram one, just one.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: One 40 milligram tablet each morning. And atorvastatin at night?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Codeine. It makes me very sick.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you. Is anything else going on? Any wounds or sores?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The district nurse dresses a sore on my left heel twice a week.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay. I can't examine you over the phone, but this sounds like a tummy bug. My main worry is that you're getting dry, and some of your tablets can affect your kidneys when you're dehydrated.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh dear.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: While you're unwell, I'd like you to stop the metformin, the ramipril and the furosemide. Restart them once you've been eating and drinking normally for 24 to 48 hours. Keep taking the atorvastatin.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'll write that down.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Try to drink small amounts often, a few mouthfuls every 10 to 15 minutes. Rehydration sachets would help.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd like a blood test tomorrow to check your kidneys. I'll ask the district nurse to take it when she comes to do your heel.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: That's good.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If you can't keep any fluids down, become confused or very drowsy, pass no urine for 12 hours, or you see blood in the diarrhoea, call 111, or 999 if she's very unwell.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay. Thank you, doctor.

reference_note.history: Vomited twice this morning, none since lunch; four to five loose stools today. No blood in stools. Crampy abdominal pain before defecation. Poor oral intake. Last passed dark urine this morning. Postural dizziness. No falls (the fall mentioned by her son was a neighbour's). Tired but not confused, per son. District nurses dressing a sore on the left heel twice weekly.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Metformin 500 mg twice daily. Ramipril 5 mg once daily. Furosemide 40 mg each morning (initially said two tablets, corrected to one). Atorvastatin at night. Codeine intolerance (vomiting).
reference_note.examination: Telephone consultation; not examined. Son reports she is making sense.
reference_note.impression: Probable infective gastroenteritis with dehydration in an 85-year-old on metformin, an ACE inhibitor and a loop diuretic; risk of acute kidney injury.
reference_note.plan: Sick day rules: temporarily stop metformin, ramipril and furosemide until eating and drinking normally for 24–48 hours; continue atorvastatin. Small, frequent fluids; oral rehydration sachets. U&E blood test tomorrow (district nurse to take at heel dressing visit).
reference_note.safety_netting: Call 111 (or 999 if very unwell) if unable to keep fluids down, confused or very drowsy, no urine for 12 hours, or blood in stool.

mutations.seeded_rationale: A tenfold furosemide dose would cause severe dehydration and kidney injury if given, though it would likely be questioned.
mutations.description: Furosemide dose ten times too high

mutations.original_text: Sick day rules: temporarily stop metformin, ramipril and furosemide until eating and drinking normally for 24–48 hours; continue atorvastatin.
mutations.seeded_rationale: If the sick day rules are undocumented, her family and the district nurse may keep giving a diuretic, ACE inhibitor and metformin to a dehydrated 85-year-old, a common cause of acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis.
